Palm Leaf Crafts

Handmade Palm Leaf Coasters in 20 Minutes

Four strips, twenty minutes, and a set of six handmade palm leaf coasters. The fastest useful thing you can weave, plus how to make them match.

11 September 2025 ME By Maya Ellis 6 min read 898 words
Share

On this page

  1. The one move you need
  2. Making the set match
  3. Drying and care

In short

Four strips, twenty minutes, and a set of six handmade palm leaf coasters. The fastest useful thing you can weave, plus how to make them match.

Coasters are the best possible first project. They are small, they are finished in twenty minutes, and you end up with something you will use every single day rather than a lump of half-woven leaf in a drawer.

Make one to learn the move, then make five more to match. A set of six takes just over an hour once you have the rhythm.

The whole coaster is four strips and one weave. Two strips run one way, two run the other, and each loose end folds back over the edge and tucks under. That is it. There is no base to turn, no wall to raise and no rim to fold, which is exactly why it is the right place to start. The only reason a coaster fails is uneven tension, so aim for snug rather than tight, and check the square after every strip by laying it flat on the table. If it rocks, one row is tighter than the other, and you can still fix it before the leaf dries. It is also worth weaving one coaster as a test piece before you cut a whole set, so you can check your strip width and your tension without wasting good leaf on a size you do not like.

What You'll Need (per coaster)

  • 4 palm leaf strips, 1.5 cm wide and 25 cm long
  • Sharp scissors
  • A shallow bowl of water
  • A clothes peg
  • A heavy book for pressing the finished set

The one move you need

Step-by-step instructions

  1. 1

    Lay the uprights

    Place two strips vertically, 1.5 cm apart, and peg them at the top. Cut the tips at a slight angle so they slide through the weave more easily.

  2. 2

    Weave the first row

    Weave a horizontal strip over the first upright and under the second. Push it up tight against the peg so it cannot drift while you work.

  3. 3

    Weave the second row

    Weave the last strip the opposite way, under the first upright and over the second. You now have a small square with four loose ends.

  4. 4

    Tuck the ends

    Fold each loose end back over the edge and tuck it under the row it meets, so it lies flat on the underside. Trim to about 5 mm past the edge.

  5. 5

    Press flat

    Stack the finished coasters under a heavy book for a day. They dry flat and stop curling at the corners.

  • Aim for a finished square of about 9 cm, which suits a standard mug.
  • Cut all strips to the same length first, so the set matches.
  • Tuck the ends to the underside, never the top, so the coaster sits flat.
  • Keep the finished ones under the book while you weave the next.
  • Make six, because guests never use just one.

Making the set match

Six coasters only look like a set if the leaf matches, and the only reliable way to match leaf is to cut every strip from the same frond on the same day. Two fronds cut a week apart will never quite agree, and the difference shows when they sit side by side on the table. Cut all twenty-four strips at once, keep them under a damp cloth, and weave them in one sitting if you can. If you must spread it over two days, store the uncut strips in a cloth bag with a damp cloth so they stay workable. Even a small difference in the age of the leaf shows up as a colour shift, and once six coasters sit on a table, that shift is the first thing anyone notices. If you only have one frond, make four coasters rather than six and keep them a true set.

Drying and care

Coasters are small enough that they dry quickly, which is both a blessing and a trap. Left on a table in a warm room they will be dry in half a day, but they will also curl at the corners, because the outer edge dries faster than the middle. Press them between two boards under a stack of books as soon as they are woven and leave them for a full day, and they will come out dead flat. Once dry, a light rub of beeswax on both faces makes them resist a sweating glass, and a wipe with a barely damp cloth is all the cleaning they ever need. Never soak a coaster and never put one in a dishwasher, because heat and water will soften the weave and pull it out of shape.

Helpful Tips

  • If a coaster curls as it dries, mist it lightly and press it again. It will flatten in a day.
  • For a rounder look, trim the four corners at 45 degrees after pressing.
  • Weave a whole set from one frond so the colour matches. Two fronds cut on different days will never match exactly.
  • A drop of beeswax on each coaster makes it water-resistant enough for cold drinks.
  • Stack the pressed coasters flat in a drawer. Rolled or bent, they take the curl straight back.
  • Weave a spare coaster or two while you are set up. They cost minutes and they make a good small gift.

Twenty minutes in, you have a coaster. An hour in, you have a set of six. This is the fastest way to end up with something genuinely useful from a single frond.

Frequently asked questions

How long do palm leaf coasters take to make?

About twenty minutes each. A matching set of six takes a little over an hour once you have the rhythm of the weave.

Are palm leaf coasters waterproof?

Naturally they resist a little, but a coat of beeswax makes them properly water-resistant. Wipe spills promptly and never leave them sitting in a puddle.

Why do my coasters curl at the corners?

They dried too fast, usually in sun or near heat. Mist them, stack them under a heavy book for a day, and they will flatten and stay flat.
